title: Pulse-Controlled Topologically Protected Quantum Batteries
authors: Jin Yang, Biao Xiong, Jibing Liu, Houguo Yu, Dehua Liu, Feng Mei, Chuanjia Shan
abstract: Quantum batteries have emerged as a promising new generation of energy-storage devices for powering quantum technologies. Long-distance charging is particularly attractive because it minimizes interference between the charger and the battery, thereby attracting considerable interest. Here, we propose a topologically protected long-distance charging protocol for quantum batteries based on a pulse-controlled superconducting qubit chain. By dynamically modulating the pulse-mediated couplings, we realize topologically protected energy transfer from the charger to the battery. We show that the charging process is free of energy backflow and remains robust against imperfections in pulse control. Moreover, the energy stored in the battery at the target time is fully extractable, and the protocol remains effective for relatively large system sizes. To further accelerate charging, we optimize the pulse shape and elucidate the underlying physical mechanism. Our pulse-controlled topological quantum battery protocol provides a versatile framework for implementing long-distance topological charging and establishes a theoretical foundation for designing optimal-control strategies to enhance quantum battery performance.
summary: This paper proposes a novel, topologically protected method for charging quantum batteries over long distances using a superconducting qubit chain modeled by the SSH Hamiltonian. By dynamically controlling the couplings with optimized pulses, the authors ensure efficient, directional energy transfer that is robust against noise and imperfections. This establishes a theoretical framework for enhancing quantum energy storage devices.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing a robust, long-distance, and topologically protected charging protocol for quantum batteries.
main_result: They demonstrate that pulse-controlled topological charging can achieve complete energy transfer free of backflow, and this protocol remains robust against system imperfections and noise.
method: The study uses theoretical modeling based on the SSH model and analyzes the time evolution of the system's zero-energy eigenstate using time-dependent Hamiltonian techniques.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a one-dimensional SSH-type qubit chain where the ends act as the charger and battery. The dynamics are controlled by time-dependent pulse-mediated couplings, allowing the system to adiabatically switch between edge states.
key_observables: Charger energy ($E_C(t)$), battery energy ($E_B(t)$), extractable work (Ergotropy), and the adiabatic ratio ($C$).
important_parameters: The control pulse shape (cosine vs. tangent) and the disorder strength ($W$) are key parameters used to test robustness and acceleration.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the adiabatic approximation, which requires the rate of change of couplings to be slow compared to the energy gap between eigenstates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SSH chain setup, the energy spectrum evolution, the time dependence of energy transfer, and the robustness of the zero-energy state against disorder.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the topological framework using the SSH model to implementing the charging protocol via pulse control, and finally analyzing the performance and robustness against noise using optimized pulse shapes.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum energy storage and transfer, which is highly relevant to quantum computing hardware development, particularly in superconducting qubit architectures.

It is observed that, within a certain range of W, the presence of disorder has little eﬀect on either quantity. However, when W becomes too large, both EB(tf) and EB(tf) decrease with increasing W, with the extractable work being more severely aﬀected. This indicates that disorder does alter the quantum state ρB of the battery.
